title: Response Tier Catalogue Playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight playbook for categorizing and exposing response tiers (aka "lanes") as a first-class product primitive in the Redwood API. The goal: give application teams simple knobs to trade latency, cost, and fidelity in predictable ways, with telemetry and rollout guidance baked in.

Why now:
- Lots of teams are building tiered experiences (fast preview vs deep answer, costed assistants, archival lookups) but each reinvents a config.
- We can standardize lanes (names, guarantees, telemetry) and ship runtime + SDK defaults so product teams adopt without long infra work.

High-level concept:
- A "response tier" is a named configuration that maps to: model variant, decoding strategy, cache policy, batching preference, affinity to dedicated capacity, and fallback policy.
- Exposed as: response_tier: "flash" | "steady" | "deep" | "archive" (string enum) on the generate/chat/embedding endpoints.
- Each tier has explicit SLOs and cost buckets (expected latency P50/P95, relative cost weight).

Proposed tier catalogue (initial):
1) flash
  - Purpose: immediate, interactive UI where latency is primary (e.g., realtime suggestions, typeahead).
  - Mapping: small model or distilled variant, greedy/low-sampling decoding, max tokens small, prefer hot cache and local dedicated pools.
  - SLO: P50 < 60ms; P95 < 200ms for short responses (<40 tokens).
  - Cost weight: 0.3x baseline.
  - Use cases: autocompletion, inline helpers, chat presence.

2) steady
  - Purpose: default balanced tier for customer-facing responses where quality matters but low cost is desirable.
  - Mapping: medium-size model, standard sampling (top_p/top_k), standard timeout.
  - SLO: P50 < 300ms, P95 < 800ms for typical responses (~100 tokens).
  - Cost weight: 1x baseline.
  - Use cases: web chat, default assistant replies.

3) deep
  - Purpose: high-fidelity, research/explanation support, code outputs, multi-step reasoning.
  - Mapping: large/full model, higher sampling or ensemble/rerank, KV-preserved long-context, allow longer token limits, optional CPU fallback gating.
  - SLO: P50 < 800ms, P95 < 2s (depends on length).
  - Cost weight: 3x baseline.
  - Use cases: code generation, reports, complex reasoning.

4) archive
  - Purpose: cost-optimized retrieval/embedding/semantic-search responses where latency is non-critical.
  - Mapping: quantized models, batch processing, aggressive caching, background wake-ups.
  - SLO: best-effort; useful for async flows.
  - Cost weight: 0.15x baseline.
  - Use cases: nightly vectorization, background summarization, archived transcript queries.

API sketch (minimal):
- request body additions (optional):
  {
    "response_tier": "steady", // string
    "tier_constraints": { "max_cost": "0.5x", "max_latency_ms": "500" } // opt - advanced
  }
- Defaults: if omitted, treat as "steady". SDKs will surface constants and helper functions.

Runtime contract (developer-facing guarantees):
- A tier is a policy, not a hard promise. We will aim to honor SLOs for median traffic profiles.
- If platform cannot meet a tier (e.g., capacity spike), automatic fallback rules apply: try same tier on different region, then degrade to next lower fidelity tier, then return explanatory error.
- Telemetry will always include: actual tier used, fallback chain, latency, token usage, cost estimate, and artifact ids for tracing.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- API accepts response_tier param and returns used_tier in response metadata.
- Console shows per-tier P50/P95, cost-per-1000-requests estimate, and a simple "what changed" note for model mapping.
- Runtime honors basic mapping for dev/p0 tiers (flash, steady, deep) in hosted mode.
- SDKs expose constants and a client-side optimizer helper (pick_tier_for_prompt(prompt_profile)).
- Docs: one-pager + examples for migration.

Telemetry and metrics to track:
- Per-request: requested_tier, used_tier, fallback_steps, latency_ms, tokens, token_cost_est, model_variant.
- Per-customer: mix of tiers used, cost per tier, errors per tier, % of requests falling back.
- Experiments: show retention/engagement lift when switching to higher tier for targeted prompts.

User stories (examples):
- As a PM for our chat widget, I want short UI hints (flash) to be instant so typing feels snappy, while long answers use deep so quality is higher.
- As a platform engineer, I need a single knob to route heavy background jobs to archive pool to reduce cost.
- As a customer using dedicated capacity, I want to bind "steady" to my reserved GPU pool and ensure SLOs.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) internal alpha (2 weeks): expose param in internal staging, route flash/steady to existing small/medium models; collect telemetry.
2) public beta (4–6 weeks): documentation, SDK flags, optional enable by customer account; add console visual for tier usage.
3) GA (timebound): support deep/archive mappings, SLA language for dedicated, per-tier cost guide and auto-suggest in Optimize.

Experiment ideas:
- Tier-aware prompt rewriting: small transformer that rewrites prompts to be cheaper for flash (truncate, compress) and more explicit for deep (expand context).
- Adaptive tiering: server-side policy that upgrades/downgrades tier based on recent user engagement signals (e.g., if user clicks "more detail" then rerun on deep).
- Per-route default tiers + per-user overrides.

Safety and failure modes:
- Misconfiguration could surface poor quality under "flash"—add clear client warnings and "sanity-check" tests in SDK.
- Billing drift risk if customers unknowingly request deep at scale; console alerts and quotas per tier.
- Privacy: ensure archive tier honor data retention/KMS rules; explicit mapping for private deployments.

Open questions (short):
- How do we version tier semantics? (tier v1 allowed behaviors may change as runtimes improve)
- Should explicit cost weights be exposed as numeric billing multipliers or only shown as estimates?
- Policy for dedicated customers: do we allow per-tenant override of tier-to-model mapping?

Back-of-envelope token economics (example):
- baseline = steady = 100 tokens = $0.01 per request.
- flash (0.3x) => $0.003, deep (3x) => $0.03, archive (0.15x) => $0.0015.
- Goal: enable product teams to reason about expected spend with simple multipliers.

Next steps / TODOs (me + collaborators):
- [ ] write a concise API spec (Kai) — include examples for generate/chat/embedding.
- [ ] prototype server-side fallback chain and log shape (Evan).
- [ ] console mockups: per-tier usage, cost, and quick-assign (Maya & Zoe).
- [ ] small user study: ship to 3 internal teams and gather feedback on tier names and defaults.

Notes to self: keep tier names friendly and non-technical for product teams, but have technical aliases internally (flash -> t1, steady -> t2, deep -> t3, archive -> tA). Consider "microflash" later for sub-10ms token heuristics.

End of playbook draft — rough, intentionally opinionated. Will iterate based on runtime constraints and SRE feedback.
